cands.name: Larry Thompson

money.note: Individuals gave $10,379; PAC money $0; candidate's own money $55,952. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Entertainment lawyer, talent manager and film producer. Founder and president of the Larry A. Thompson Organization in Los Angeles. Served in the U.S. Army Reserve from 1968 to 1974. Has not held public office. Ran for Congress as an Independent in 2020 (CA-37) and as a Republican in 2024 and 2026 (CA-32).

endorsements.text: Republican Party of California (listed by Ballotpedia for 2024 and 2026)
Ventura County Republican Party, Los Angeles County Young Republicans, California Young Republicans and San Fernando Valley Republican Assembly (listed on his campaign site)
Stand With Crypto rates him "A" ("Strongly Supports Crypto"), per his campaign site

cands.gaps: We found no documented positions from Larry Thompson on data centers, new development, growth limits, protecting land and water, foreign or investor purchases of California homes and land, property taxes on homes, school choice or teacher pay, or H-1B visas. His stated positions come from his own campaign site and Ballotpedia survey answers, not from independent interviews. The Los Angeles Daily News questionnaire and the local news items listed on his site were not available to read. He has held no public office, so there is no record of official actions. The campaign site's issues page was cut off partway through, so his later positions were not read. His abortion statement was left out because it does not fit a simple for-or-against reading: he says he is personally against abortion, wants states to decide, and opposes a federal ban.

cands.bio: Democrat and U.S. Representative for California's 32nd District. First elected to Congress in 1997. Lawyer and CPA who served on the California State Board of Equalization, including as its chair. Sits on the House Financial Services and Foreign Affairs committees.

controversies.text: Federal records show $27,900 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $662,131 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26.
Missed 18 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (2.7%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 11, 2025-01-09 to 2025-01-16.

In December 2017, McClatchy reported that eight former aides said Sherman's Washington and California offices were so uncomfortable that junior staff felt unable to raise harassment concerns about former aide Matt Dababneh. Sherman called himself "a demanding boss" but denied that his management style contributed to the silence about Dababneh's behavior.

endorsements.text: California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO (2026)

cands.gaps: We found no stated position or action from him on data centers, homestead property tax relief, limits on institutional or foreign buyers of homes and land, H-1B visas, school vouchers or charters, or teacher pay. We found no documented stance on development or data centers specific to a project. He did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey in 2020, 2022, 2024 or 2026. His campaign site's issues page was cut off partway, so later sections (such as Israel, Armenia and LGBTQ+ issues) were not fully read. No foreign-government ties were documented in the pages we had. The pages gave no detail on his early-life upbringing beyond Southern California schooling.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

qual.background: Lawyer (Harvard J.D.), Certified Public Accountant and Certified Tax Law Specialist, with Big Four accounting experience. Elected to the California State Board of Equalization, which he chaired from 1991 to 1995. Has served in the U.S. House since 1997, on the Financial Services and Foreign Affairs committees.
qual.why: He has about three decades of legislative office and earlier statewide elected tax-board service, plus law and accounting training. That puts him in the high band for lawmaking, oversight and budget work.
qual.label: He has about three decades of legislative office and earlier statewide elected tax-board service, plus law and accounting training. That puts him in the high band for lawmaking, oversight and budget work.

second-amendment.evidence: His campaign site says he cosponsored the Assault Weapons Ban, the Bipartisan Background Checks Act, Ethan's Law on safe storage, and the Federal Extreme Risk Protection Order Act, which encourages state red flag laws. It also says he holds an NRA 'F' grade.

pro-life.evidence: His campaign site says he works to protect abortion rights and Planned Parenthood funding. Wikipedia describes him as pro-choice and says he called the overturning of Roe v. Wade 'appalling and outrageous'.

slow-growth-protect-land.evidence: In 1997, while on the House Budget Committee, he authored the Sherman Amendment to the budget resolution, which added $700 million for acquiring environmentally important lands in FY 1998.

back-police-order.evidence: His campaign site lists investing more in 911 emergency response, including for firefighters and police, among his priorities.

workers-first.evidence: He voted Nay on the Laken Riley Act, which required DHS to detain certain immigrants without legal status who are arrested for theft-related crimes. It passed the House 263-156.

prio.label: Matches 2 of 5 priorities; 2 backed by their record, 1 only promised
